To-morrow is July 26, and I should like to ask the Minister of National Revenue if he will see that these values for duty purposes are established to-morrow.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. B. RYCKMAN (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: In answer to the hon. gentleman I may say that I will discuss the matter with my colleagues.

Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 113, to amend the criminal code.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time . and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Parading while nude.

I am confident that all
hon. members will be in accord with this amendment, the primary purpose of which is to provide more fitting punishment for a
fanatical class of Doukhobors who defy our Canadian laws by gathering on public highways and in close proximity to the highways in an absolutely nude condition. I want to give members of this committee what might be called a close-up view-
Oh, oh.

I hope the chairman will
understand that I am speaking metaphorically when I say I want to give hon. members a close-up view of this fanatical class. While hon. members may get some amusement from it I should like them to understand that this is a very serious situation.
These people were brought to Canada as far back as 1898. They were bonused to come here; a huge acreage of land was set aside for them in Saskatchewan and the government went to considerable expense in placing them upon that land and getting them started. Shortly after 1900 a large number came to the district of West Kootenay and settled in that beautiful valley along the Kootenay river between the city of Nelson and the Columbia river. To-day in that district there are some three thousand of these people, who are divided into three groups. First there is the community group, living in one section and directed by their leader, Peter Veregin. And then there is an independent group composed of Doukhobors who have purchased land of their own and withdrawn from the community. Then there is a third or fanatical group who are usually known as the sons of freedom. They lead the procession in these nude parades and exhibitions.
The three peculiarities of Doukhobors and particularly of the fanatics are these. First of all, there is arson, they do not hesitate for one moment to burn anything. Their second peculiarity is nude parading. And the third is defiance of the law'. They have absolutely no regard for Canadian law. First of all they burn schools; they burn churches; they dynamite public halls. The department of the Postmaster General has before it now a claim for damage done to a federal post office which was dynamited only a short time ago. Then they show their defiance of the law by refusing to register births, deaths or marriages. Nobody knows who is who among these fanatics. They proceed in this country on the assumption that the land is God's land and they know no laws but God's law. They do not intend, therefore, to subject themselves to the laws of any province or of the Dominion. When I say they refuse to pay taxes, I mean that they refuse to contribute to the community treasury for the payment of taxes on community-owned land.
Criminal Code

To bring to the house the seriousness of the situation I may point out that the party represented by hon. gentlemen opposite are responsible for the coming to Canada of these Doukhobors. They brought them here; do not let them forget that. They have a lot to answer for. These people were brought in in 1898, when they were given land and a cash bonus. In 1912, after the Conservative government had come into power, they said, "We want no more Doukhobors." They are invading all the fields of labour. They know no hours of work, and no rates of wages. In 1912 the Conservative government put up the bars. They said they would have no more of it. And that prohibition continued until 1928, when the right hon. gentleman opposite (Mr. Mackenzie King), anticipating an election and thinking they might be of great help to his party, took down the bars again. But immediately this government came into power they stopped the further entry of Doukhobors.
We realize that the provincial government is responsible for the enforcement of law. But there are circumstances beyond which it is impossible for a provincial government to go. The costs are too great, and if the truth must be told-and I say this advisedly-these people are numerically too strong for this government or the provincial government to keep them within bounds. I have always contended and still contend that the federal government, having brought them here, must share the responsibility for their conduct and the cost of their maintenance while here.
Hon. gentlemen think it trifling for me to refer to fires, but it is not an occasional fire that takes place. I have just received from the Minister of Education in British Columbia a list of schools which have been burned, and the information will be almost appalling to the house. I will mention only those fires that have occurred from June 1929 to the end of the year. In that time they burned seven schools valued at $14,700. They were small country schools. In April 1930 they burned a community hall valued at $2,500. On July 1-it will be seen that these fires are close together-they burned another school valued at $2,200, and the same night they dynamited a brick school which cost $7,700. And then we come to Christmas of 1930. At a place called Thrums they were preparing the Christmas tree. A boy got out of a oar with a basket of toys and tree trimmings, and just as he was proceeding to the hall the place blew up. It was only his lucky detention for a few minutes that saved his life. Now we come to March 1931-that is since

we have been here. In that month three schools were burned. On June 2 they destroyed one and attempted to bum another, and they burned the Presbyterian church. These fires all take place at about the same hour, eleven o'clock at night. They cut the telephone wires and take particular care to avoid discovery.
I have another letter from the Minister of Education in British Columbia, which gives a good idea of the situation. He states that-by reason of these fires it is necessary for all schools to be guarded. In his letter of June lr he says:
I am quite sure that if the guards were taken away the schools would all very shortly be burned.
He cites this particular school at Krestova in the district adjoining mine, where he says the fire started while two Canadian teachers were asleep in the building.
As for the statement that the cost of the provincial government is too great, I would point out that the loss by fire in this district in the past two years amounts to a total of $50,000. These fanatics have destroyed schools, churches and community halls to that value. And in the rampage of 1929, to arrest the Doukhobors and keep them in gaol six months cost the provincial government $35,000. There you have $85,000 of actual loss and expenditure to govern a community of some 4,000. Hon. gentlemen who live in places with a population of about 3,500 know that the policing of such places does not cost more than $5,000 per annum.
I want to come now to the matter of community parades, and I am sure I shall have the most rapt attention.

What do you mean,
"rapt"?
"Unwrapped", I should say.

Let me explain. This does not mean one person here or there disrobing for the benefit of passersby; the fact is that these people gather in groups of fifty and seventy-five, marching along the highways and through the fields. And in other instances they make special exhibitions.
Oh, oh.

This is not a laughing
matter. I want the committee to appreciate the seriousness of it. During a recent convention of the farmers' institute, one whole morning was spent discussing the seriousness of this situation. It might come home more closely to hon. members if they had their life savings tied up in a ten-acre plot of ground

Criminal Code
and a Doukhobor came along and bought the land alongside. Only one thing can be done- move out.
There was the great rampage of 1929 and then another only a few weeks ago. The last letter I received from this district states that !he Doukhobors are again on the rampage. One lady writes me that as her children were coming from school they were confronted with a number of naked Doukhobor men and women. She tells me of two little girls who were on their way to her house and who came rushing in frantic and shocked by the fact that two naked Doukhobor men had accosted them on a public highway. The committee will remember the recent rampage into Nelson when 108 of these naked Doukhobors were placed in gaol. They had started a trek of some ten miles and as they approached Nelson the fire trucks and all other kinds of trucks and wagons were used to barricade their way.
Carried.

It will not be carried for
a while. Twenty-four special constables were sworn in to assist the provincial police. One of these constables had a naked Doukhobor woman on each arm, and they just picked him up as if he were matchwood, laid him down on the road, and sat on him, one on his head, and one on his body.
Carried.

If we could take some of the long, thin hon. members opposite or some of the short, thick ones and put them down in the middle of the road on a hot August day with two naked Doukhobor women weighing 300 pounds sitting on them, then they would probably realize that these people are beyond control of the law.
Oh, oh.

I am glad to hear hon. members laugh because such laughter reflects the attitude of indifference taken during the last six years by both the provincial and federal governments. These Doukhobors have burned churches, school houses and buildings; they have tom the uniforms from inspectors, the tunics from police officers and the clothing from federal enumerators. They have used sticks of cordwood on the provincial police; they defy the law by refusing to contribute to the provincial treasury. They refuse to register births, marriages, and deaths, and they practise and preach open defiance to Canadian law.
This is the description of a situation almost inconceivable in Canada, and yet these are the people by whose votes the right hon.
gentleman opposite (Mr. Mackenzie King) hoped to defeat the Conservative candidate in West Kootenay. Some of these people enjoy the franchise because they were born in Canada, and I ask the committee if it can conceive of the great Liberal party being reduced to the extremity of encouraging such a class of people to vote. The Liberal workers went out into the hills and valleys to bring these people to the polls to vote at the last federal general election. On the morning of election day the Conservative candidate published a statement that he did not want a single Doukhobor vote, and I am proud to say that he did not get one. When the right hon. gentleman publishes his memoirs I hope he will include a picture of this memorable happening on July 28 last. Just imagine a milling mass of men and women who could not speak English with the Liberal workers showing them how to mark their "X" after the name of the Liberal condidate. These Doukhobors were receiving their orders from Peter Yeregin, so that one man controlled the votes of 1,500 people. They were challenged, but challenging did not do much good because it was impossible to know who was who. The scrutineers did not know what their names were or where they came from. All oaths had to be taken through an interpreter and when the polls were closed there were 600 Doukhobors on the outside trying to get in. The Conservative agents saw' that the polls were closed on time, and that oaths were administered to all who applied for ballots. The Conservative candidate polled two votes from returned men who happened to be agents there. The Labour man got one vote, and-

speechtext: I think the hon. member should confine his remarks to the section before the committee.

This is the hon. member's speech of the session.
Criminal Code

I am referring to the
amendment to the criminal code which provides for a three year term in the penitentiary in place of the six months' imprisonment which is now the penalty for Doukhobors who go naked. If this amendment had been in force two years ago, these naked fanatics would not have been able to vote for the Liberal candidate.
The provincial government has amended its elections act to disqualify from voting any Doukhobors or others, male or female, born in the province or elsewhere, who claim exemption from military service. These Doukhobors were admitted to Canada unconditionally exempt from military service. I look to this government to bring in a similar amendment before another election is held. Those who are not willing to fight for their country, should not be permitted to run it. If this amendment is not effective, I would suggest that in so far as the men are concerned, other means should be taken to restrain their exhibitions. Perhaps the most effective means would be the lash. Some citizens have suggested that these people should be placed on a couple of islands out on the Pacific.
I am sure that the committee, after hearing what is the true state of affairs, will take a more serious view of the Doukhobor situation in this country. I know some hon. members may get some amusement out of this, but let me tell them that the men, women and, indeed, whole families who are* subjected to these obscene exhibitions are not in a very comfortable position. I am sure if hon. members lived amongst these Doukhobors they would feel just the same as do those who complain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This clause in the bill
has been drafted to meet a situation which has certainly a very serious aspect. The actions of a particular portion of the community known as the Doukhobors, more especially in British Columbia and perhaps also in Saskatchewan, have become nothing short of a menace and an insult to all right thinking people who live in certain portions of those provinces. The matter has been brought to the attention of the Department, of Justice by the government of British Columbia, particularly by the premier and the attorney general, and also by certain organizations and individuals of that province. The description of these nude parades as related to the committee by the hon. member for West Kootenay who has just taken his seat, has not been overdrawn. I have heard similar stories from officials of the province of British Columbia. The trouble
[Mr. Lapointe.!
is that the section of our criminal law which now applies to indecent exposure is not sufficient in the way of penalty to stop these parades. The present law provides that a fine of $50 and a term of six months' imprisonment at hard labour may be imposed. The provincial authorities have had many prosecutions and both fine and imprisonment have been imposed, but this has not had the desired effect on these fanatical people who insist on carying on these nude parades.
It has been suggested by those who know the situation best that if the penalty were increased as proposed in this bill to a maximum of three years' imprisonment, probably the most fanatical of this particular community would be made to respect the law. They look upon the shorter term of six months a3 more or less of a holiday and as no very serious punishment at all, and they openly boast that they are being kept at the expense of the province. It is suggested that these penalties be increased. I think the committee will agree that these nude parades as they take place.now in these Doukhobor communities, should be stopped. They are, as I say, an insult and a menace to the right thinking people who live in those particular portions of Canada. With that end in view these amendments have been prepared; I think we have covered the case as fully as we can in the language we have used, and I would ask the committee seriously to consider these clauses.
What would the minister consider necessary in the way of clothing so that a person will not be liable under paragraph (d) ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The last sentence provides it.
It is pretty vague.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, it is not. It reads:
For the purposes of this subsection anyone shall be deemed to be nude who is so scantily clad as to offend against public decency or order.

But that will leave it
pretty much to the discretion of the judge as to what sort of costume offends against public decency. After all, we have heard much about the Doukhobors this afternoon, but this clause does not mention them at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. It applies to anybody.

It might be made lo
apply to bathers at many fashionable resorts. I think my hon. friend will agree with me on that. There are people who are more severe and strict in their views of this than

Criminal Code
others. I am quite sure some judges would find that a certain bathing suit does not accord with public morality, whereas others would find the same costume absolutely correct. I know there is a difficulty in striking a proper description of what would constitute a crime, but I am afraid the clause as it reads is a little vague.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think we can depend upon the discretion and good sense of the judge who hears the case. In many instances under our criminal law we have to depend upon the good sense of our judges and juries
We have to help them though.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The language of the clause is:
Anyone shall be deemed to be nude who is so scantly clad as to offend against public decency or order.
That is taken in connection with the foregoing that they must be parading.
It does not apply to parading at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Just a minute. Let me read:
Everyone is guilty of an offence and liable upon	summary	conviction	to	three	years'
imprisonment who, while nude,
(a)	is found in any public place in company with one or more-
There must be at least two. A single individual would not be prosecuted.
Yes, under paragraph (a) but not under paragraph (c).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The clause reads:
Everyone is guilty of an offence and liable upon	summary	conviction	to	three	years'
imprisonment who, while nude,
(a)	is found in any public place in company with one or more persons who are parading or have assembled with intent to parade or have paraded in such public place while nude, or
(b)	is found in any public place in company with one or more other persons, or
(c)	is found without lawful excuse upon any private property not his own, whether alone or in company with other persons, or
(d)	appears upon his own property so as to be exposed to the public view, whether alone on in company with other persons.
The last two paragraphs referring to a person appearing alone upon his own property or upon that of his neighbour would be sufficient.
Does that apply to public theatricals and theatres? I do not see anything which protects them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It applies only to places mentioned in the bill.
A theatre is sometimes a public place.

I am quite in sympathy with what the hon. member for West Kootenay has said. I saw the parade of the Doukhobors from Yorkton some years after they had arrived in this country. They came through the constituency of Marquette and one cannot compare the wearing of bathing suits with their nudity. I have seen bathing suits from Hollywood and I have also seen these Doukhobors parading through the constituency of Marquette, and the sight of the Doukhobors was most appalling. I am quite in sympathy with driving out of my part of Canada those individuals who will parade nude through the streets. We rounded these men up in Minnedosa and shipped them back to Yorkton. I am sorry my hon. friend has them in Kootenay.
Might I press my question on the Minister of Justice as to whether there is any protection for theatres?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no need of protection for theatres.
Do people need to go nude in theatres in Montreal?

But some of those who
appear on the stage are, to put it mildly, scantily attired.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If they offend against
public decency, they come under this measure.
That is a question of opinion. To some they offend against public decency where as to others they do not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is in the discretion of our judges and juries.

Is it the intention of the
minister to make the penalty three years for a first offence, or not exceeding three years? The way it reads, a first offender would have to receive a penalty of three years,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Three years is the maximum penalty, but any less penalty may be imposed.

The Minister of Justice said just now, quite properly, that we could always trust to the good sense of judges and juries, but these people are not going to be tried by judges and juries, but upon summary conviction by one or more justices of the peace, and three years' imprisonment is a very heavy penalty to be left to the discretion of two justices of the peace. I do not know any
Criminal Code

other section of the criminal code where the penalty is three years' imprisonment on summary conviction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes. Police magistrates or justices of the peace have power to impose very long terms, much longer than three years in many cases.
Is it not a fact that paragraphs (a) and (b) as distinguished from paragraphs (c) and (d) are to exempt the individual who parades in a public place alone in the nude.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Paragraphs (a) and (b)
refer to more than one person. Paragraph (c) would include one person or more than one person, and so would paragraph (d).
So if an individual paraded in the nude in a public place alone this section would not apply?

What about turkish baths
and places of that sort?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That would not be a
parade, as I understand it. It comes under paragraph (c) or (d) if he is alone.

It seems to me that the
second part of paragraph (d) is loosely drawn. I agree entirely with the Minister of Justice that certain people might think that certain bathing costumes are all sufficient while others would have bathers put on dress which would be just about as good as jumping into the water with your clothes on. It seems to me that something should be added there to protect bathers who appear in the ordinary costume.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not quite catch the last part of the question.

It seems to me that
something should be added to this clause to free from penalty in any shape or form those who appear in reasonable bathing costume.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The last clause is intended to apply to them. This is only intended to apply to people who are nude or so scantily clad as to offend against public decency. In reply to the suggestion of my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre there might be an improvement made there by adding after the word "place" in the first line of paragraph (a) and after the word "place" in the first line of paragraph (b) the words "whether alone or," so that it would read "is found in any public place whether alone or in company with one or more other persons." I move accordingly, Mr. Chairman.

Might I ask whether the first paragraph does not cover sufficiently the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre? Anyone appearing singly in a public place nude comes under the provision with respect to a person doing an indecent act where the public have access.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That carries only a six
months' penalty.
I suppose the idea was that stronger penalties were to be provided for these parades. The first subsection already provides for the ordinary act of indecency by a single person.

It seems to me that under paragraph (b) a justice of the peace who had strong views as to the amount of clothing a bather should wear could enforce drastic penalties if he so desired, on the ground that they were scantily or indecently clad.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is an appeal against that.

Yes, but you are making these extreme penalties applicable, and the law now is sufficient to protect against that sort of thing.
Amendment (Mr. Guthrie) agreed to.
Was there any definition in the criminal code before of the word nude?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. Nude has, of course, a meaning. It means without clothes, naked.

I think some difficulty arises in connection with paragraph (d). Recently a magistrate in Toronto expressed the opinion that a woman would not be properly dressed for bathing unless She was covered from her neck to her knees. Few modern bathing suits would comply with that requirement, yet that particular magistrate would probably find justification in this clause for imposing a very severe penalty for those who were not so clad.

Section agreed to.
Sections 3 and 4 agreed to.
On section 5.-Publication of false advertisements to promote sales, etc.

It seems to me that 'there is a contradiction in terms in this section. It says "contains any statement of fact which is untrue." Now a fact is a fact. A fact contains the truth, and a statement of fact or an enunciation of a fact must be true. It seems to me there is inconsistency there, and

Criminal Code
I was going to suggest something of this kind to carry out the intention, to substitute for the present language the words "what purports to be a fact, but which is untrue, deceptive or misleading."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We could meet that difficulty by simply striking out the words "of fact."
It might be a statement of law, and then we would have to go to the privy council to find out whether it was true or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is another consideration with respect to this section to which I would direct the attention of the committee. Formerly the penalty was provided for one who "knowingly" publishes, and the real change that is made here is to strike out the word "knowingly." The question has been raised by 3ome very prominent business people in Canada as to the propriety of striking out that word, and of putting a saving clause at the end of the section. They represent that many bona fide advertisers are mistaken in some of the statements they make, through no fault of their own in many cases, and that it is hard to penalize them for statements innocently made. The difficulty with the word "knowingly" in the clause as it now stands is that it imposes upon the prosecution the burden of proving that a certain thing was stated knowing it to be false or untrue, and very often the prosecution is not able to prove that knowledge on the part of the accused, and consequently the prosecution fails. If the word "knowingly" is struck out the section becomes much broader, as the committee will see. It has been suggested that a saving clause to this effect should be added at the end of the section:
Provided further that in any prosecution under this subsection a case may be dismissed if it be established to the satisfaction of the court upon proper evidence that the accused acted in good faith,-*
In other words, if it can be proved that he did not knowingly mislead by the statements he made. If this amendment were put in, the onus would be upon the accused to show that he had acted in good faith, and if he had so acted and convinced the court of that fact the court might forgive him of his offence. In the present section the word "knowingly" appears and the result is that prosecutions have failed because the crown has not been able to establish the fact a man has knowingly inserted a false advertisement, knowing it to be false. The amendment was originally asked for by many clubs, better
business associations, boards of trade and the like in Canada. I have no very definite views upon the subject, but I must say that the saving clause I have suggested might be advantageous.

Would it be added to
the present proviso?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, at the end of the
present section. Then as my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has pointed out, I think an amendment might be made by changing the words "which contains any statement of fact which is untrue, deceptive or misleading" to the words "which contains any statement which is untrue, deceptive or misleading."
That is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We would be striking out the two words "of fact" in line twenty-nine of section 5 of the bill.

Does the minister so
move?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have merely made a
statement to the committee.

The only point I see concerning the words "statement of fact" is that such statements might be considered by the courts in contradistinction to statements of law. It is usual and proper to talk about statements of fact as distinguished from statements of law without implying that a statement of fact is per se true. The words "of fact" are used in contradistinction to show that a statement of law is not intended. I had thought that was the intention of the amendment. If so I believe the words should be left in the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think the words are of great importance, one way or the other. My hon. friend from East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) may be right. We do not however find statements of law in connection with sales of goods. I would not pay much attention to the suggestion of my hon. friend in that connection. I think if the words "which contains any statement which is untrue" are in the section they will be sufficient to cover the points in question.
Yes.

I wonder if by removing
the words "of fact" merchants who advertise reductions from $4.00 to $3.99 would be affected. Such advertisements would in fact be untrue, deceptive and misleading. Yet he would not be making a statement concerning the kind of goods advertised.

If a merchant cuts his
price, what more is there to it?
That is not misleading.
That is not what the act is intended for.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I prefer that the words
"of fact" should remain in. If, however, the committee prefers they be struck out I have no serious objection.

I am not a lawyer and I
cannot express a legal opinion, but from the standpoint of an ordinary man the expression that a statement of fact is untrue is absolutely absurd.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, it is not absurd.
There are statements of fact and statements of law to which reference is made every day in courts. On statements of such and such a fact comments may be made, and on statements. of law other comments are in order. Certainly there is a distinction.
I am speaking as an ordinary layman, not as a lawyer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think the section is particularly affected, no matter which way we leave it. I prefer that it should remain as it stands, but if the committee thinks the words "of fact" should come out, I have no obj ection.
Strike them out.

In the section before us
there is protection for newspapers, but no protection for the ordinary printer who publishes circulars.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is referring to the publisher of advertising circulars which are passed around?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This section provides
only:
Provided that any newspaper publishing any such advertisement accepted in good faith in the ordinary course of its business shall not be subject to the provisions of this subsection.
I think the words in the section ought to meet the case my hon. friend has in mind.

The printer who, in good
faith, publishes a circular should in law be protected as much as the newspapers.

Would not the minister consider an amendment which would extend to the persons who caused to be published any particular advertisement? For instance, a real estate man might in good faith advertise that

a railroad was going to pass through a particular town. Time might prove that his statement was deceptive. The amendment proposed by the Minister of Justice apparently applies only to newspaper publishers. Should not such protection be given to a person who causes an advertisement to be published?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The man who caused it

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. members for
Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne) and York-Sun-bury (Mr. Hanson) have, I submit with deference, quite overlooked the fact that under our system of jurisprudence appeals are not to be taken in criminal cases beyond the court of last resort in the province. Up until recent times the principle has been that in criminal cases there should be no appeal upon any question. Of course, the privy council always retained the right to review a criminal case from any part of the king's dominions if it were found that justice had not been administered by due process of law. It was then decided that there should be an appeal in criminal cases on questions of law only, but the principle of our jurisprudence was that that right of appeal ended in the province. However, it was believed that if there was a dissenting judgment on a question of law, there should be a right to go to the Supreme Court of Canada. It will be observed that the dissenting judgment must be on a question of law. As the former Min-22110-263i
ister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has just said, it is now being provided that the principle of an appeal not going beyond the province is still being maintained, but where there is dissent with respect to a question of law, then the supreme court shall decide as to the validity or invalidity of the dissent.
If this whole matter is opened up we would be going contrary to the general rule and be wholly opposed to our system of jurisprudence. It will be recalled that in the two addresses delivered by the Lord Chief Justice of England when he visited the Canadian Bar Association, attention was drawn to the practice and procedure and the functions of the court of criminal appeal in Great Britain. In that case there are provided by statute certain questions which shall be considered by the court, but in a broad and general way this matter resolves itself into this: that the court of appeal shall not review the findings of fact by a jury-'that is the prerogative of a jury and not a court-the questions of fact having been decided, the only question which remains is as to whether or not, during the trial of the prisoner, the law has been properly interpreted to the jury. This question involves the legality of the reception of evidence and the propriety of the judge's charge to the jury. If an appeal is taken and there are one or more dissenting judges, it seems to me to be not unreasonable to ask that the dissent should be clearly indicated so that the question of law upon which there has been a difference of opinion should be settled by the court of last resort.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	The notes of the dissenting judges are not produced in the supreme court. As I understand this section, the practice will be to limit the appeal strictly to the points of law upon which the dissenting judge and his brothers have differed.

I submit that there have been cases and will be cases in which the majority of the court of appeal has been and may be wrong. Unfortunately I was not in the chamber when this section was under discussion. I have been a good deal in touch with the Doukhobors ever since they have been in this country. I learn there has been considerable levity in the committee concerning these people and it is for that reason I think a few words should be said on their behalf. Only some 8,000 Doukhobors
Criminal Code

came to this country about forty years ago. 1 do not know what the natural increase has been, but I suppose at the utmost there would be only 15,000 or 20,000 in the country to-day, a certain number of them in Manitoba, a much larger number in Saskatchewan, a few in Alberta and quite a large colony or several colonies in British Columbia. I think it is only fair that the phblie generally, perhaps especially the eastern public, should not be prejudiced against this group of people, who on the whole are very excellent citizens. The fanatical group among them is comparatively small. They constitute a very small proportion of the. entire number of Doukhobors. It is quite true that the whole group have some very peculiar characteristics. They may be said to be the Quakers of the Greek Orthodox church. They came into existence many years ago because of their attitude towards the state-they were opposed to the use of arms-and also because of a protestant attitude towards some of the evils then existing within the Greek church. Essentially they are a group of high-minded and heroic people, so much so that they attracted the attention of Count Tolstoy, who learned a great deal of his philosophy and of his special viewpoint of Christianity from these selfsame Russian peasants. In fact he was so much interested in them that I understand that a good deal of the proceeds of his book Resurrection went to assist in bringing the Doukhobors to Canada.
It ought to be understood then that the Doukhobors are not a lowdown, degraded people. Let me give the house one illustration. Several years ago I was asked to participate in a conference of young Doukhobors held on the plains of central Saskatchewan. The members of this conference consisted of students attending the various educational institutions-high schools, normal schools and the university. The leader of the group was a graduate of Saskatchewan university, and a lawyer of good standing in the city of Saska-'toon. His wife, a very charming woman, is the daughter of a former professor of Queen's university. They have a beautiful home in the city of Saskatoon. I admit that that is an exceptional family, but the fanatical ones are also exceptional, and it seems to me very unfortunate that the public of Canada should be given the idea that the Doukhobors are simply a troublesome, degraded set of people. On the whole the vast majority of them are living clean, decent, honourable hard'-working lives. Several years ago when some of the local residents at Nelson, not liking the fact that a great many of the Doukhobors bought 
wholesale instead- of patronizing the local merchants, got up a petition to the British Columbia government, a commission was appointed to investigate, and it found that there was no crime amongst them and no poverty, that ithey were among the best citizens of the province. That gives some idea of the other side of the question.
I quite frankly admit that this small group about which we hear so much has created a good deal of difficulty. They are fanatical. I am not quite sure whether they are mentally sound, but as with many such religious sects they are subject to hallucinations and queer ideas, and undoubtedly a number of them have broken the law in this country. They have burned down schoolhouses, and in the early days some of them burned their implements and went on a crusade eastward to Winnipeg and a little further east. Those pilgrimages are examples of the fanatical side of this religious movement.
Let me further point out that this curious practice of disrobing is not one that arises because of some perverted emotion or lax sexual ideas. Nothing could be further from the truth. In the beginning as practised some years ago it was rather a religious practice. Those who know anything about the history of fanatical religious sects may remember certain groups among the Protestants in the New England states who were guilty -if you call it "guilt"-of very similar practices in the early days. With these Doukhobors the idea seemed to be in the beginning that in some way they had to get back to primitive conditions, to show that they were not dependent on all the various trappings of civilization. I am inclined to think that in more recent days they have resorted to this practice as a sort of protest since they found that it annoyed the authorities, and called attention to some of their grievances. But I would impress on the house that this practice is not the outcome of immorality as we commonly understand the term.
Further, may I point out that the present generation of Doukhobors have been born and brought up in Canada. If they are guilty of practices that are considered antisocial or that are not desired in this country, we can no longer deport them because most of them are native-born Canadians. That brings me to the real difficulty, that in the past we have largely neglected all of these classes of immigrants. I know that the public schools have done magnificent work among the non-English speaking people, and they have attempted to do some work among the Doukhobors, and have accomplished much

Criminal Code
good work in Saskatchewan. I remember that fifteen years ago I was talking to one of the school inspectors in the district occupied by the Doukhobors in British Columbia, and he said that about the only reason he was interested in trying to establish schools among the Doukhobors was in order that at least a few of them would be able to defend themselves from the exploitation of some of the people round about them. In many respects he thought the comparatively simple life they were living was a very desirable one. I am not making out this particular fanatical sect as being all we would desire, but I would say that we ought to have some knowledge of the background of these people in order to understand some of their fanatical acts.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I was asked a little
while ago to bring back the hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) to the question before the committee, namely, amendments to the criminal code. Of course, my hon. friend is speaking with the consent of the committee, but I would not like it to be thought that I was prejudiced in allowing my hon. friend to speak when I had to stop another hon. member.

I shall not trespass on the courtesy of the committee very much longer. I was suggesting that we must understand the background of these people. One reason why they try to get away from the enumeration of the census is that they fear that they may be brought under military conscription, which is fundamentally opposed to their religious convictions. Further, their idea seems to be that they are a peculiar people, and should be let alone as far as possible to live out their own community life -a sort of imperium in imperio.
Undoubtedly one difficulty has been that they have not been very fairly treated in the past by some of the authorities in this country. Some years ago when they first came to this country they were allowed to live together, holding and working their land in common. That was their understanding of the condition under -which they had migrated. Then there came a change in .the department. A Minister of the Interior was appointed who did not know or care about the previous arrangements, and he forced them or tried to force them to make individual entry and to live as other Canadians were doing. They refused to do that, and there was taken from them at that time land that was valued at something like $10,000,000. They feel, on account of some of these experiences, that they have not been dealt fairly with in Canada. Repressive measures which from time to time have been used against them have not improved the situation.
I have no particular objection to the bill. I suppose that the citizens of this country have to take some means of maintaining Canadian standards along these lines, but I would suggest that this way of dealing with a problem of this kind is not going to be effective. We are not really touching the problem. What we have to do is in some way learn to understand these people, understand their point of view, do a good deal of educational work among them, and not consider that merely by repressive measures we will overcome these deep-seated religious instincts and social practices which have been prevalent among this particular group for at least several centuries.
I venture to bring these considerations before the committee first as a protest against the idea that this particular fanatical sect represents the whole of the Doukhobors, secondly to counteract the idea that they are any more immoral than any other class of people, and thirdly in the hope that either this parliament or some other group of people in Canada would adopt a more constructive way of dealing with these people whom we have admitted to our country. They and their problems undoubtedly will be with us for years to come.
I wish to express to the committee my appreciation for allowing me to speak at this stage.

I should not like the suggestions of the last speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) to go without some measure of challenge. Let me make the point perfectly clear that this amendment to the criminal code is not directed at any group of people anywhere who have observed even the laws of common decency dear to the heart of all persons living under what we might term western civilization, and in the temperate zone. I will admit that in the tropics conditions might be different. I should not like the idea to go forth, either, that these people are the victims of repressive measures. My hon. friend himself remarked that the Doukhobors have been in Canada for approximately forty years. During that time they have been under the control of a series of governments. That is, different parties have been in control both in the provinces and in the Dominion. I think I can say without exception that of all the people who have entered Canada from the outside none has

received such patient consideration as this particular sect known as the Doukhobors. Neither at this nor at any other time have the authorities directed repressive measures against a single Doukhobor who observed- I will not say the laws, because few of them really observe our laws in spirit-but who have been free from doing violence to all sense of decency in this country.
My hon. friend states further that they have been forced into this course of action to defend themselves against exploitation, and as an illustration he said that the business men of Nelson were jealous of the Doukhobors because to some extent they had succeeded in establishing a communal system. There may be personal opinions, but as a matter of fact there has never been any effort by any authority to interfere with these people in their peculiar economic theories and ideas.
I was trying to say that complaints of t'he business men of Nelson had led to the appointment of the British Columbia commission.

But my hon. friend took care to leave the impression with the committee that because the business men of Nelson were critical of the communal system they had inspired a certain amount of unfavourable or-shall I say-repressive action. That is not the case. Generally speaking I would say these people are thrifty. They are hard working and administer their affairs well. Those of us who know them fully recognize that fact. Speaking of the Doukhobors around Grand Forks, Brilliant and Nelson those who observe the amenities of civilization, shall I say-and they are in the majority-are looked upon as thrifty and decent settlers, and as such are welcomed in the community. Those are not the people however at whom this legislation is directed.
We have been forced to the action we are now taking. Why? Because for forty years the people of Canada have patiently endured some of the most absurd spectacles, some of the most ludicrous efforts on the part of a group of fanatics to enforce their own peculiar notions and idiosyncrasies. In the present instance however we have something more than that. To-day in Grand Forks, Brilliant and Nelson there are men who owe allegiance directly to the present communistic system existing in other parts of the world and who are taking advantage of their innocence, if you like, the ignorance and prejudice of these people to lead them into an anti-law method of activity or system of action in the province of British Columbia.

To-day they are being led by that class of people. My hon. friend spoke concerning a family and drew a picture of what might have been one of the most cultured families in Canada. His picture described a highly educated people, and he stated further that none of the present generation indulged in the practices to which the bill refers. What are the facts?

Again I interrupt.
I did not say that none of the present generation indulged in these things.
I took those words down.

My hon. friend
misunderstood me. I said that most of the people who indulged in these actions were born and brought up in Canada and could not be deported. My statement was exactly opposite to my hon. friend's understanding.

My hon. friend drew a
very attractive picture of a cultured family. Let me tell him and this committee that what has brought the present action to a head has been recent activities taken by the group to which he refers in connection with the taking of the census. Who were the people who began these latest mischievous and ludicrous nude parades? It was a group of young girls just out of high school who met the census takers who had gone patiently to interview them. If necessary I could show correspondence to prove my statements, but I state that those census takers went to those people, day after day, even going to the extent of taking some of the saner ones with them to try to get the required information from the people they were interviewing. We did not care so much about getting all the answers, but it was our desire to learn their names so that they might be properly enrolled. What did they do? Led by some of the educated young women who were graduates of the high school at Vernon, British Columbia, they commenced to disrobe right in the public place when the enumerators appeared. It is that sort of thing which has brought the government to take the rather extreme action proposed by the present legislation.
My hon. friend has very charming diction; his voice and language are always excellent and tuned to convey the precise view he wishes to express. I notice he said in a very minor key, "some have disregarded the law." "Some have disregarded the law"-Mr. Chairman, hundreds have disregarded the law. They gathered in mobs which were described this afternoon. During the last two years they have dynamited schools, post offices,

Criminal Code
community halls, and the grave of the late Peter Veregin. There is grave suspicion, although probably not definite proof, that while on a train, one member of the local legislature was bombed. While in the Doukhobor section a bomb was placed under his seat. There has never been at any time in connection with any group in Canada so much violence as has been practised by these people. The patience and tolerance of the rest of the people in the neighbourhood has been simply phenomenal, I think. I do not think my hon. friend can cite a case where the people in the localities in which these outrages have occurred, the Canadian people who are entitled to some consideration and some modicum of protection by the law, have risen up and attempted to resent with violence the action of these people. It is true that when a nude parade started into Nelson, consisting of hundreds of these fanatics, either last year or the year before, action was taken. These people marched right to the city of Nelson; they were not residents of that city but were simply thrusting themselves into the town with their nudity and their crudities. Were the people of Nelson to stand idly by and do nothing? This is what happened: The chief of police and the mayor of the community called on the people for help; a number of special constables were sworn in, and they met these fanatics at the edge of the town and herded them off the main streets. In some cases fire hose was used to prevent their advance.
My hon. friend is not doing justice to himself or to this house when he seeks to leave the impression that in introducing this clause in amendment to the criminal code the government is in any sense using what he terms repressive measures.
Are these not repressive measures?

My hon. friend went on
to say that this disrobing practice was a sort of religious rite. There is very little about it that is religious now, although that may have been the case two centuries or ten centuries ago, in the early history of these people. Certainly it is not a religious rite at the present time; it is done absolutely for provocative purposes. When these people are faced with an effort on the part of the officers of the law to enforce some simple respect for the law, immediately this disrobing practice begins, because they know it is one of the most embarrassing things with which an officer can be confronted.
I am not going to say anything more other than to remind the committee once more
that if we are to protect our public buildings and institutions and the sane, respectable and law-abiding citizens of this country from the outrages which are perpetrated by a faction of these people, if you like to call them that, then we must have more teeth in the law in order'to enforce it. We-and when I say "we" 1 mean Canadian citizens generally-have been more than patient with these people; I do not think any country in the world would have tolerated this sort of thing as long as it has been tolerated in this country. Certainly they would not have received any such consideration south of the international boundary, and I doubt if there is a country in Europe where they would have been treated so leniently. Talk about repression; talk about religious rights; there is not a country in the world where there is more general liberty given the people to indulge in their own peculiar religious beliefs than is the case in Canada. I do not know of any instance when the Canadian people, regardless of the law, have interfered in this respect, but I want to say that we Canadians owe some duty to our families and to our own people, and this amendment is designed as something which will enable us, under the law and with constitutional authority, to do that which hitherto we have not been able to do.
I may say that I would much prefer to have this difficulty overcome by other means. Never, until this moment, have I uttered a word against the Doukhobors in this country, though I have been m pubic life for some years. I have vainly hoped that, as the years went by, it might be possible to win these people from some of these mad practices in which they indulge, but these outrages have become so common that I have given up that hope. They continue to indulge in this obscene practice, it is nothing more; if my hon. friend wants to get further particulars he has but to go to the inner records of the department which would not make a very savory recital here. If he will look up those records he will get away from the idea of a gentle, devout religious observance to a true appreciation of the obscenity of many of these practices and these nude parades. It is most unfortunate that we have to discuss the matter here, but certainly those in authority must be given some power and some weapon with which to protect the decencies of Canadian life.

What I have to say will not take very long, and it is rather important; my hon. friend, Who lives in the west, could profit by the lesson himself. We have been filling our country with the scum of the world through paid and bonused immigration, and to-day we must admit that if we had followed the policy of filling our country with our own Canadian citizens we would not have been obliged to pass laws such as the one now under consideration. I think, as a Canadian, it is my duty to say that governments in the past were most guilty in adopting that open door immigration policy, which meant an open door immigration to the scum of the world and a closed door to immigration coming from the old provinces of Canada, especially from the province of Quebec.

Will not the hon. member admit that the great majority of those immigrants are loyal, valuable and useful citizens of Canada?
Mr. LaVERGNE:	Certainly; I will admit
that, but now we have proof that while we were receiving immigrants from all the different races of Europe we had not the necessary population to assimilate them. Here we have a small group of eight thousand or ten thousand people who have been here forty years and who are not assimilated as yet. Not only have they not adopted Canadian institutions; they have not adopted western civilization, and I claim we should profit by the lesson. Chickens are coming home to roost; I think "chickens" is the proper word, after the illustration we had
IMr. LaVergne.]
given us this afternoon of young girls disrobing before census enumerators. If the fair name of Canada has been spoiled it is our own fault. We should have been more careful with our immigration; we should have opened our door only to races which could be readily assimilated. I repeat what I have said for the last thirty years, that the best immigration is that which comes from within our own country. We should have settled our western provinces with Canadians or with such races as the British or the French from the other side of the Atlantic who, until about twenty-five years ago, were barred by the policy of the government, to-day it costs less for an immigrant to come from Europe and settle in the west than it does for a Canadian from Ontario or Quebec to go and settle there. These facts should open our eyes, and instead of quibbling and raising points of order we should try to put into force a broader, a cleaner and a more Canadian policy for the future.

speechtext:
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide that the governor in council may authorize the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of the sum of five cents on every bushel of wheat exported from the provinces of Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan of the crop of 1931, and to make provision for the determination of amounts payable thereunder, and for regulations to carry out the purpose of the act and prescribe penalties to be incurred for breach of the act or regulations.
He said: The bill to be founded upon this resolution provides for the payment of 5 cents a bushel in ithe provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. It is proposed that the money shall foe distributed through the machinery of the Board of Grain Commissioners, and that it shall be paid' to the person who is the producer of the grain. It was hoped that some provision might foe made for following the grain through Canadian vessels to the ports of ultimate shipment, but although we were very' strongly urged to have such a provision in the resolution and in the bill it was found as a practical matter impossible to do so. The lake shipowners urged it very strongly, as did the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Simpson), but there was no machinery by which we thought it could be done. Therefore the payments will be made direct by the elevators through the machinery of the Board of Grain Commissioner's. If the house will go into committee on the resolution and allow the matter to be advanced a stage or two, there will be full opportunity' to discuss the bill in committee.

The resolution is somewhat different from the statement in the budget address. On that occasion it was intimated that the freight was to be absorbed on all wheat shipped for export, meaning abroad, I suppose. The resolution, as I understand it, includes interprovincial trade. As I see it, the local mills in each of the three western provinces will be discriminated against. If a farmer wishes to sell, say to ithe Robin Hood mill at Moose Jaw, or to any other mill in the west, he will not be eligible for the 5 cents if the mill is in his own province. So that the farmer or other seller will not sell to the local mill unless
he gets 5 cents more per bushel than the ordinary market price. The only means by which the seller could get the 5 cents would be to sell to a mill in an adjoining province or for export abroad. If he sells to a mill in another province, under the terms of this resolution he will be eligible; if he sells to a mill within his own province he will geit nothing. Should the local mill take his, the farmer's wheat and pay him the ordinary price plus the 5 cents the miller will be at that disadvantage with competitors both abroad and interprovincially. That is the way it appears to me.

Prime Minister give his reasons for proposing this resolution?

speechtext:
There are three reasons.
The first is the low price of wheat in the markets of the world. It is a well known fact that the sudden collapse of the wheat market brought about a condition in western Canada which is being felt all over this country, particularly in eastern Canada. This section of the country relies to no small extent upon the purchasing power of the western population, and this purchasing power has been so lessened by the reduction and diminution in the price of wheat that it has assumed almost national proportions.
The second reason is brought about because of the first reason. The price received for the grain does not bear that relation to the cost of production which it did heretofore.
The third reason is the necessity of a measure of relief for western Canadian producers. I have been told by those who are better able than I to speak with authority that the effect of this measure will be excellent and that it will lessen the amounts which we may be called upon to pay for direct relief in cooperation with the provinces.
Then there is the psychological effect which perhaps the hon. member will not underestimate. The great wheat producing areas of Canada lie between the lakes and the mountains. It is the products of that territory which have given Canada a reputation abroad as a wheat producing country. A population discouraged by a great reduction in the price of their products and because of a calamity which lias overtaken them as far as successive crops are concerned, will be heartened by the fact that to this, extent the parliament of Canada recognizes their situation. Perhaps the bill founded upon this resolution will give a better explanation than can be given in a
Bonus on Wheat

mere sentence or two. It is proposed to utilize the machinery of the grain act, and the money will be distributed through that agency directly to the people who are affected. I learned only yesterday that in the opinion of those interested in the grain business the effect upon whose who have lost their crops will be very considerable, even though they will not benefit. There are many other reasons for this resolution which I could mention, but I think perhaps the hon. gentleman understands why this legislation is proposed.

The latest report is that there are 100,000 who will require relief because of an absolute loss of :rops.
The right hon. gentleman has given four reasons for" this legislation. The first reason is the low price of wheat; the second reason is the low price when compared with the cost of production; the third concerns relief, and the fourth is the psychological effect. I fail to see any real reason why the government should adopt a sectional policy such as this. If relief is to be given, why not make it general. I think I am within the judgment of the committee when I say that we who live in other than the western provinces have refrained from placing before the house the situation which confronts the farmers in our provinces. The condition in almost every section of the province of Ontario with which I am familiar is such that at the present time it is almost impossible for a farmer to make ends meet.

Mr. Chairman, before we go into the details of this measure, I think we should first discuss the general principle. In all probability during the discussion of details some hon. member opposite will rise and ask us if we are in favour or opposed to this measure. That is the kind of criticism which has been levelled against us. The Prime Minister has given certain reasons for the introduction of this measure, and at this stage I accept them as good reasons. In spite of what the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) has said, I do not think that the condition of the farmers in the three western provinces can be compared with the condition of the farmers in Ontario, Quebec, and other provinces of the Dominion. The latter, although they are suffering from low prices, have the promise of an abundant harvest. But even before conditions had been aggravated as they were by the drouth in the west, the farmers in western Canada suffered very severely from the drop in prices. Although the Prime Minister may at the present time take the position that these serious conditions are the result of what has arisen during the last few months, I take this opportunity of stating, as I did on a former occasion, that even before present conditions arose, the situation in the west was very severe and perhaps the Prime Minister by this time realizes that fact.
I am quite willing to admit that the reasons which have just been mentioned by the Prime Minister are good ones. The burden has rested very heavily upon the western provinces. A short crop last year in many sections and a very low price meant that in many cases farmers were due to lose their equity in their farms, and since they were bearing in a special degree the burden of those low prices, it seemed to me well that the whole burden should not be borne by the west but that part of it might be borne by the people of Canada. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASED PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION
speechtext:
Convinced as I am of the merits of the bill, and having listened attentively to the reasons brought forward by hon. members opposite who opposed it, I wish to make a few remarks so that if the bill does not pass the responsibility may rest in the proper place.
This bill was not presented to the house because of the fancy of the hon. member for Compton, or through political motives, as was suggested by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), but because of a necessity existing in connection with butter. As I stated on a former occasion the matter of adulterated butter came before the annual convention held last fall of the dairymen's association of the province of Quebec. May I say that that convention brings together a body of men representative of the dairy industry in that province. At the meetings of that convention there are about 55 or 60 inspectors of cheese and butter factories of the province, the heads and officials superior to those inspectors, the directors and professors of the dairy school at St. Hyacinthe and several of the factory owners in the province. Certainly that body of men is in a position to give an opinion as to what should be done in the best interests of the dairy industry. This question was brought before the board of directors, of which I have the honour to be a member, and the board finally came to the conclusion that the adulteration of butter could not be stopped with the existing penalties. Therefore the board passed the resolution which I read on a previous occasion, and that resolution was brought before the convention, where it was adopted. As a result, Mr. Chairman, this bill was presented.
I was amazed at some of the reasons put forward by some hon. members opposite in opposition to this bill. The hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Girouard) discussed the various subsections of section 5. I might remind the hon. member and the
Dairy Industry Act

committee that these subsections are exactly as they were previously; not one word has been changed. I would also remind the hon. member that the act which is being amended was passed by this house in 1928, when the Liberal government was in power and when the hon. gentleman was sitting on this side of the house. Certainly he had every opportunity to discuss these subsections at that time, and if they were not in the best interests of the dairy industry they should have been amended when the original bill was passed.
One of the principal objections to the bill was that we should give more latitude and more discretion to judges in the application of the law. As I said in the beginning, those who have had the responsibility of making complaints and trying to secure convictions were of the opinion that the existing penalties were not sufficiently severe to stop the adulteration of butter, and the discretion allowed the judges is just as it was before this amendment was introduced. There again not a word has 'been changed; the judge can impose anything from the minimum fine to the maximum fine, so it only remains to decide whether or not those penalties are sufficient. That is the reason this bill has been brought forward, because the men in the trade claim that these penalties are not sufficient to stop that adulteration.
Another objection put forward by hon. members who oppose this bill is the question of good faith on the part of those who produce butter. I do not blame the hon. genltle-men; they would like to convince their electors that they are safeguarding the interests of the butter makers, so they say it would be too bad if some farmer or butter maker who produced butter with more than 16 per cent of moisture content should be fined S500. Surely this cannot be a question of good faith. The man who buys 400 or 500 pounds of butter, puts it in a mixing machine and adds 200 or 300 pounds of oil certainly cannot plead good faith. But they ask, "What about those who are found with more than 16 per cenlt of water in their butter?" I say, Mr. Chairman, that not one of those people has been convicted under section 5 o'f this bill. I hold in my hand the record of convictions for 1930, which numbered 91. Of that number 71 were convicted in connection with butter containing over 16 per cent moisture, while 18 were convicted for the real adulteration of butter. Of the 71, all were convicted under the section of this bill which provides a minimum fine of $10 and a maximum fine of $50, and the officers of the department here tell me that over 90 per cent of those convicted were fined

the minimum of $10 and costs. Of the 18 who were found guilty under section 5, all were convicted because they had adulterated butter in the real sense of the word. So I defy hon. gentlemen opposite to point to one case in which a butter maker or a farmer has been prosecuted for producing butter containing over 16 per cent moisture or less than 80 per cent butter fat and fined under section 5 of this act which I am trying to amend.
I do not desire to cast any reflection on those who oppose the bill; I take it for granted that they are capable men in their respective walks of life. The hon. member for Comox-Allberni (Mr. Neill) speaking the other day to the tariff item concerning chickens and ducks, said he found it strange that those who discussed that item were lawyers, doctors and other professional men. So, while I take it for granted that all the hon. members who spoke against this bill are practical men in their respective walks of life, yet the people who considered this question last jrear at Mont Laurier were more acquainted with the question than the hon. members who have opposed this bill. I find that of the seven or eight members who spoke against it four or five are lawyers, one or two are doctors, and one is a newspaper man. There was not one fanner in that number. Surely, Mr. Chairman, there must be a farmer on the opposite side of the house, and I should like to hear him express an opinion on this question.
