I fully realize that if hon.
members opposite wish to prevent this bill from becoming law they can easily do so. They have only to talk for half an hour and very likely the bill will not come before the house again. That is why I have made these remarks. I know that the whole dairy industry is behind the bill. Every thinking farmer is in favour of it. The main objection of hon. gentlemen opposite has been that the poor farmer who is caught with more than 16 per cent of water in his butter will be fined $500. They know that this has never happened under section 5, because the officers are very careful. Those who adulterate butter are well known; there are only a few of them in Montreal. Everyone in the trade knows them and this bill will put a stop to the practice. If hon. members who represent rural constituencies are sincere in their criticisms they will allow the bill to become law.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASED PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION
speechtext:
I have just a few words to say on this bill. My hon. friend from Compton (Mr. Gobeil) will admit that in Quebec there is a distinction between butter factories and creameries; they are not at all the same thing. The butter factory is the place where in the country they make butter, and the creamery is where it is made in the city. This is a very important distinction. I regard it as an evil that so much milk is being sent to-day from the country to the city for manufacturing purposes. I do not think that many hon. members will contradict me on that point, because some business is needed to encourage the farmers and give them every chance in their struggle. It is unfortunate that in Quebec as no doubt elsewhere, factories are being closed because the farmers are sending their milk to the city 22110-264
instead of having it made into butter or cheese in the locality. How is that done? My hon. friend from Compton, who is a director in dairy societies, must know that the creamery people falsify the records, giving to the producer less fat than he is entitled to and then raising the price. It is a fake, and is done to deceive the farmer. The farmer is paid for less fat than his milk contains, although the price he receives is apparently higher. That is how so many farmers have been deceived into sending their milk to the city creameries instead of taking it, as many do, to the local butter factory. This is an evil, and I submit that my hon. friend's bill, though his intention may be good, is simply un coup d'epee dans l'eau-a sword thrust in water. I suggest that the important thing would be to have some inspectors in these creameries. I have no technical knowledge of the industry, but I was told that these creameries are not as rigidly inspected as the butter factories. It is of the utmost importance, and it would be in the interests of the local buttermaker, to have these creamery factories veiy carefully inspected, to make impossible the falsification of records. If this were done the farmers would know exactly what price they were getting for their product; they would know what price the creameries were paying for a stated quantity of fat. They are entitled to know just how much fat their butter contains.
Let me tell my hon. friend that I am not ashamed of being a lawyer. I represent a rural constituency and I am proud of the fact, and I should feel that I was not doing my duty if I did not speak for them here. I have at heart the interests of those I represent. I am not making a political speech; I am speaking on the authority of people who know just as much about the industry as the hon. member for Compton. There is an evil which we must stop, and the only way to do that is, at the earliest opportunity, to amend the law, providing for the strictest inspection of creameries so that the farmers shall not be deceived. It will be just as well also to put some restraint on the farmers. The important thing is to prevent the falsification of the records. The bill reads:
Any person who violates any provision of sections five or seven of this act shall be guilty of an offence and upon summary conviction, shall be liable-
And then follow the penalties, which are heavier than those in force at the present time. What is meant by "any person"? The rural butter factory is generally operated by a single man. He is either the owner of the

Dairy Industry Act.

factory or is employed by a syndicate or society of farmers who own it. However, it is entirely different in the cities. There the creamery is usually owned by a company w'hich has a president, a general manager, several employees and lots of watered stock. Who would be responsible in that case? Would it be the president, would it be the manager, or would it be the poor employee who is acting under their instructions?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASED PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION
speechtext:
It would be the same as
before; the law is not being changed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASED PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION
speechtext:
We are here to improve
the law, and I know my hon. friend is sincere in his efforts to that end. I believe this amendment would make the law more severe without making a distinction between the factory in the city and in the country. I think such a distinction should be made. This amendment does not achieve the result aimed at. I do not know how it is in other provinces, but I know there is some trouble in Quebec city and Montreal. The people in the rural districts should be told that the reason they do not receive more money for their products is the deduction for transportation made by the creameries in the cities.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE INCREASED PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION
speechtext:
This
measure aims at increasing the penalties provided by the Dairy Industry Act. When the bill was discussed in the house some time ago, I pointed out why, in my opinion, this measure was unjust and vexatious towards the farmer. I do not intend to go over the reasons which I then gave; I simply wish to answer an objection which was raised. Some hon. members on the government side have stated that this measure does not apply to farmers. They certainly are under a false impression. It is only necessary to read the act with the proposed amendment in order /to convince oneself that the provisions apply to eveiybody, to dealers as well as farmers. It is precisely with reference to this point that I wish to make a few comments. Subsection (b) of section 5 of the act reads as follows:
"No person shall
(b) mix with or incorporate with butter, by any process of heating, soaking, rechurning, reworking, or otherwise, any cream, milk, skim-milk, buttermilk or water to cause such butter when so treated to contain over sixteen per centum of water." [DOT]
"No person shall," these words therefore apply to everybody, and, according to the proposed amendment, a person violating the section just read would be liable to a fine of $500, and, in default of payment to im-

prisonment for a term of six months. Therefore, a farmer who, in good faith, mixes with the butter or introduces in it water to cause such butter when so treated to contain over sixteen per cent of water, is liable for a first offence to a fine of $500, anil in default of payment to imprisonment for a term of six months. I state that inasmuch as this measure applies to farmers, the act is unjust and arbitrary. That is why I move, seconded by Mr. Pouliot, the following amendment:
That clause I of the present bill be amended by adding after subsection (c) of section 10 of the Dairy Industry Act, the following subsection :
(d) The present section does not apply to farmers who manufacture or sell butter made from the dairy products of their farm.
Amendment negatived.

Mr. ON ESI ME GAGNON (Dorchester) moved the second reading of Bill No. 132, to amend the Civil Service Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will not repeat what I said on Monday last when I had the honour to move the first reading of this bill. I will say briefly that one of the features of my bill is to exclude the outside service from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission.
Now, with respect to appointments, it is my desire to incorporate into the act the recommendation made in 1924 by a committee of the Senate which considered this question at length and reported to the effect that in connection with promotions the Civil Service Commission should cooperate with the government. I also wish that with regard to dismissals the ministers of the departments be given the power to make dismissals themselves. The law as it stands provides that an employee can be dismissed only by the governor in council, and I think the amendment which I have in view is not very drastic in its terms. The change I propose is very small; if a minister has no right to dismiss an employee for cause, it is of no use to speak of the powers of the government. .
As I said, I do not want to take up too much of the committee's time because I am well aware that many members on both sides of the house are anxious to express their views and that at this stage of the session

Civil Service-Outside Service
it is not probable that my bill will become law. May I add that one reason why I have presented it to the house at this stage is to enable hon. members to study it earnestly with a real desire to do justice to the country as well as to the civil service. I am proud to say to hon. members opposite that one of the distinguished members who are anxious to amend the Civil Service Act is none other than the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), who is now the chief organizer of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec. I am also proud to say that on the 24th of June those who like my humble self are anxious to amend the Civil Service Act found another champion in the distinguished leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). Let me emphasize the fact that on that date the hon. leader of the opposition stated in the most emphatic terms that he rather favoured the exclusion of the outside service from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. He went even so far as to state that in 1924 when he voted against the Spinney amendment he was wrong and he added that he now favoured the nomination of postmasters in rural districts by the Postmaster General.
I leave my bill to the earnest consideration of the house. I am prepared to discuss the matter free from party prejudice. As I said last Monday this question is not a party one because no such amendment as I have in view can be made unless all parties concur in it.

subtopic: EXCLUSION OE OUTSIDE SEKVICE FHOM OPERATION OK ACT
speechtext:
The
major portion of this bill I support very strongly. I have been a sympathetic supporter of the Civil Service Commission because I have taken time to study its functions and the work it does, but any hon. member who believes that the Civil Service Commission appoints applicants to the outside service will be sadly disappointed. Practically all that it does is to put a rubber stamp upon the recommendation of a member of some other department. Therefore I am supporting this bill first because the Civil Service Commission does not examine the application and the applicant. That is done by a member of some other department. It was a surprise to me to learn this. A short time ago I had a very good example of it. An application was made for an outside position in the district from which I come, and I had occasion to follow up that application. A returned man, who had been a resident of that district only a few months, was given first choice-although I think when a position is locally advertised, length of residence
22110-264i
should be one factor in making an appointment. The men who were named on his application as recommending him repudiated having given their names and refused to recommend him for the position. But I want to be fair. Some two months before, this man, having drifted into the district, was recommended by these three men, who were officers of the local battalion, although they had not much information as to who he was. The man was supposed to be a very good shot, and on securing the good will of these three officers he obtained their recommendation for another job which he did not get. He had given them a promise and an oath of service, both of which he repudiated and refused to carry out. When the matter of the second position came up, these men could not recommend him and he gave their names without their consent or approval. Subsequently when they were asked to give recommendations, they repudiated having given their names. The chairman of the commission says:	I do not think that is
serious, because it is a matter of his character and on a former occasion' these three men recommended him. If a man repudiates his oath and his promise, what else is left of his character and how can any man recommend him for a position? Nevertheless, the commission accepted these three names. When I asked for the letters repudiating them, the commission did not have them on file. They were put away in a little bag, but they had the former papers on the file. These papers were not addressed 'to the Civil Service Commission but to somebody else.
In addition to that, two other returned men had applied for this position, one being a graduate of the school of science-one of our best universities. I want here and now to express my disapproval of the classification made of these men by an inspector of the Public Works department. The man who had drifted into the locality, who had been there for only a few months, was given 80' per cent, while the man who was a bona fide resident, whose family had been in the district for fifty or sixty years, a returned man with a good service record, and a graduate of the school of science, was given only 60 per cent. I ask hon. members if in such a case the Civil Service Commission performed any function at all? I give it credit for having done something in the past, but examples of this kind surely will confirm one's opinion that it does not make the appointments.

Very good, then. Take the position of postmaster; that is a permanent position. Who makes the recommendation for that appointment? An official of the Post Office Department. Would it not be better to let the Post Office Department appoint their own men? As it is their inspector goes out and examines the applicants-and remember,

this is not a temporary position, but a permanent one. Upon the recommendation of that inspector, in over 90 per cent of the cases the Civil Service Commission makes the appointment. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that these are sufficient reasons why the outside service should be removed from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. It will really not be doing anything more than what we are actually doing at the present time, because as it is now each department makes its own recommendation, and upon that recommendation the commission acts.
Secondly, there are many applications made which never reach the Civil Service Commission at all. They are pigeon-holed by certain officials in the various departments. We have proof that many of these applications do not reach the commission. They are first gone over by officials of other departments, and in many cases the applications are pigeonholed and never reach the commission.
In the third place, the Civil Service Commission, having appointed the men, cannot take care of them after they are appointed. The men are dismissed without any examination or investigation by the Civil Service Commission whose employees they are. The department can simply go to work and have a departmental investigation, and out the man goes on their recommendation without any approval or disapproval by the Civil (Service Commission.
I shall not take up any more time. I contend, Mr. Speaker, that these outside appointments are not now made by the Civil Service Commission upon any examination that they conduct, the commission simply acting as a rubber stamp of approval of the recommendations of other departments.

speechtext: I had the honour of supporting the original bill passed by this house creating the first Civil Service Commission, and I have followed the work of the Civil Service Commission very closely. I was a member of two or three committees that investigated the operation of the Civil Service Commission and the Civil Service Act, but I have not the time to refer to them to-night. I think the time has arrived when the government should seriously take into consideration this civil service question, and see if a remedy cannot be found. The big civil service associations of Canada have already protested against the adoption of any such measure as is proposed by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon). Circumstances have changed since 1908 when the Hon. Sydney Fisher introduced his bill creating the Civil Service Commission, and since Sir Robert Borden sponsored his bill extending the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission to the outside service. Conditions have so changed due to the war and otherwise that the time has come, I think, when the whole Civil Service Act should be overhauled. When next we meet, and I trust we shall all meet again, I hope that the government will be in a position to give us a matured plan which will do justice to all parts of the country, to the civil servants as well as to the public.

I have no protest to make against the system enforced by the hon. Postmaster General in connection with dismissals of postmasters who are guilty of political partisanship; the act exists and it must be carried out. When a complaint is lodged against a postmaster, the minister orders an inquiry and a commissioner is specially appointed for the purpose. In the county df Bonaventure I was privileged in having the visit of a fellow citizen from Rimousk i, who carried out numerous inquiries. I have nothing to say against the work he carried out and which seems complete; he is a member of the bar and he understands his work. However, I must protest as to his method of procedure. When a commissioner, having such extensive powers, visits a village or a parish to hold an inquiry, the latter, to my mind, should be held either at the post office or in a public place. At present, in my county, these inquiries are generally held at the home of the person who has made the charge or has caused it to be laid and who, moreover, hopes to replace the postmaster in question. I think that this procedure is of a nature to lower the prestige of the commissioners in charge of the inquiry'.
I therefore contend that these inquiries should be held either at the post office-like the inquiries carried out by the inspectors of the department-or in a public place, and that a previous notice, with a reasonable length of time, should be given as to the date of the inquiry. If a postmaster thinks fit not to be present at this inquiry, it is his concern, however, some postmasters or, again, some other persons might wish to deny these charges, but they have not the opportunity because they are not notified in advance.
I have neither the time nor the desire to discuss any further these inquiries which are held in my county for I may add the old saw, "to the conqueror belong the spoils." Such is the way the matter stands to-day and it has always been so.

The other day the minister, giving a survey of his department, said they were cutting down expenses because certain railway mail services had been dispensed with owing to the change in railway arrangements. Unless you make that provision you are crippling the mail service of the Dominion. The hon.

I shall explain my point; previously a railway which gave a daily mail service, now gives but a tri-weekly service. The mail which was previously carried daily is now carried only three times a week by that railway. If you reduce the amount paid to the railway for a given section, you are forced to increase the appropriation required to give a daily service to the people who have lost three days of service by railway. If on the one hand you
reduce the means of communication by railway, you must on the other hand increase them, otherwise, and if you do not do so, you are not giving the public the same service as in the past. Now, I find no increase in the appropriation asked for the mail service by public routes. You will, therefore, not have sufficient money to give the public the service to which it is entitled and which it had in the past.
In answer to my hon. friend, I may say: when the railway mail service is curtailed, we cater as much as possible to the needs of the section affected by other services, such as motor buses, etc.

You do not follow me, I think. Perhaps, I do not express myself clearly. For instance, in my own county, take the Caraquet railway which gives, instead of a daily mail service, a tri-weekly service. That money must absolutely be voted separately. You cannot appropriate that money because you have reduced by $150,000 the amount voted for the railway service and you have not increased the amount for mail service by public routes. You have not, therefore, funds applicable to that service and the result will be that you will have a shortage at the end of the year. With reference ,to the Temiscouata case, the hon. I grant as far
as it is possible reasonable requests, and especially when we have the funds enabling us to comply with the requests thus made to us.
The minister granted my request as regards the Temiscouata mail service, evidently on the strength of my letter.

There has been a reduction of $150,000 in the item covering mail service by railway. It has been stated that this reduction is due to the curtailment of railway service, in many cases a daily service being cut down to a tri-weekly service. It is stated also that the reduced mail service is being offset by the use of buses, automobiles and teams. The vote for mail service by ordinary land conveyance has not been increased, and I am afraid the minister will be faced with a deficit. However, that is not my business; the minister will have to accept the responsibility. I would point out to him that the money voted for one service cannot be used for another.
I have no desire to take up unduly the time of the committee. I know the minister is anxious to get his estimates through. Were it not that the session is drawing to a close, I would discuss these matters in detail. There is a matter, however, to which I should like to direct the attention of the government. In this regard the minister, being a new member of the cabinet, may not be wholly responsible, but the older members were well aware of all the circumstances. An increase iii postal charges has been put into effect which should provide at least 84,000.000 in extra revenue, and if business improves as it

Supply-Post Office
should, this increased revenue may amount to practically So,000,000, which would wipe out the deficit. During 1929 and 1930 the then opposition, now the government, blamed me for not heeding the demands of the rural mail carriers for an increase in salary, but no provision has been made in the present estimates to grant such an increase. During the' last election circulars were broadcast throughout the length and breadth of Canada in which I was depicted as having a heart of adamant because I would not listen to the cry of these poorly paid servants of the government. As it is expected that this session will close by the end of next week, there is not the time available to go into this matter in detail, and therefore I will leave aside all contentious discussion. The estimates will not permit of increases being paid this year, but I hope the government will remember its promise and grant these increases next year.

Since the house has
decided to stay in continuous session and inasmuch as none of us seems to have any business to return to, for the first time this session I propose to take up only a few minutes in order to ask the Postmaster General to see to it that a little heart or soul or cream of human kindness is put into that great post office machine. It is true, as the ex-Postmaster General has said, that a square deal for the rural mail carriers was advocated by many on this side of the house, and I suppose I really led in that matter. It seems too bad that of all the public servants in the Post Office Department, the rural mail carrier is the only man who has, every four years, to tender for his position. The man in the city who to-morrow morning dons a suit of clothes paid for by the Post Office Department, walks around a few hours, goes out in the afternoon and walks around a few hours more, receives SI,400 or $1,500 and two suits of clothes a year and has a retiring allowance; but the fellow who hitches up the old .mare and drives over the muddy roads or snowbanks gets the least consideration of all. I have advocated a square deal for these rural mail carriers. The ex-Postmaster General is correct when he says that this party is on record in this respect, and when the finances of the country become more buoyant, when the deficit in the Post Office Department is wiped out, we shall look to the present government to give some relief to the rural mail carrier.
I do not intend to take this matter up in detail; I am going to give the Postmaster General just, two examples. I took the exPostmaster General to task in connection
with this case: In a little village in my constituency the rural mail carrier, who got nine hundred and some dollars for his route, had to travel a certain distance to the post office. Later it was moved a short distance. The Post Office Department sent a public servant, who was getting possibly $3,000 or $4,000 in addition to liberal travelling expenses, to measure that distance, and it was discovered that the poor mail carrier by virtue of the moving of the post office had to travel thirty-one rods, a few feet and a couple of inches less; therefore they reduced his salary by something like $11.37! These figures are not exact, I may say, but they are approximate. In other words, the Post Office Department spent perhaps $100 out of the treasury of Canada in giving a highly paid public servant a beautiful trip in order to cut a few dollars off the wages of a struggling mail carrier. That is the general principle against which I wish to protest. It is a twopenny-ha'penny business. That was the ex-Postmaster General; this is the present Postmaster General.
It is the same law.

Yes, the same law. In
the village of Belgi-ave in my constituency a gentleman was getting ninety-five cents a day for making three round trips to the railway station, a distance of almost a mile, or I believe they call it seven-eighths of a mile. Then one train was cut off, and this man was immediately notified that because he had to make only two trips to the depot instead of three, by some rule of thumb or Chinese mathematics his pay would be reduced by thirty-two cents-I am not talking by the book-and he would receive sixty-three cents a day for making those two trips. Such action is beneath the dignity of this administration. No administration can do such a thing as that in regard to any one of my constituents, whether he be with me or against me. This man, of course, will not accept the reduction; the job will be put up for public tender, and if I can do anything in that community to have the present Postmaster General pay $2 a day for that work, let me assure the committee I will do it.
As regards the general principle, we have been trying to "keep up with the Joneses" in this country and the Jones family has wrought havoc in private life. We are spending hundreds * of thousands of dollars on the air mail service, which was a little toy for the ex-Postmaster General to play with. We need very little of that except in the hinterland or for taking the mail to those who live in the far-flung parts of Canada.
Supply-Post Office

The idea of sending a bird with a broken pinion from Toronto to Montreal when there are several fast mail trains a day between those two cities! To do that is absolutely foolish. It is an expenditure I cannot condone in the face of the fact that the man who gets up at. five o'clock in the morning receives only sixty-three cents a day for making two trips to Belgrave station. I do not know how the department figures it out. This man has a capital expenditure just as any financial or business organization has. He has himself, a horse, a 'buggy and a cutter to finance, and simply because he makes only two trips instead of three the horse cannot get along with three shoes instead of four or with two meals instead of three. I do not know by what method it is computed that this man shall have one-third of his pay cut off. I am not blaming the present Postmaster General; he is new in the saddle; he has his feet in the stirrups, and by another year we shall expect him to be an expert rider. I am prepared to give the present Postmaster General a chance, but I resent any such picayune, twopenny-ha'penny paring as has beep going on in connection with men who carry the mails from town post offices to depots. Why is it that because a train is temporarily taken off in the summer their pay is immediately reduced?
I have one case in mind. Go to the department and they will say to you: If two trains come in fifteen minutes apart, that is one trip. If a man is driving a bus, his passengers are supposed to wait because of His Majesty's mails, while the money that should be spent on the rural mail service is spent in the air from here to yonder. The man has to keep his passengers sitting in the bus or make a special trip. I wish t'o ask the Postmaster General to look into this and see that those hard and fast rules, those little regulations of the Medes and Persians that have been left on his doorstep, those little vexatious things, are corrected. The idea of cutting a man's pay from ninety-five t'o sixty-three cents and then letting millions go through the hopper without a word of protest! Before the items are carried may I ask the minister whether it is the policy of the department to give contracts at a very reduced rate to school boys to carry the mail between stations and post offices when there are married men and returned soldiers who have applied for that work? The present Postmaster

That is the most flagrant piece of robbery I have ever known to be practised on the people of the constituency I have the honour to represent. Men with families are refused work which a school boy obtains at a price of $480. His parents would not sign a contract for four years, so the term was changed to two years. The matter to which my hon. friend has referred is not one of policy, but is of a purely legal nature. If the boy is too young I understand he had no right to make a contract, and when a complaint is made the matter will be investigated.

I am surprised ito hear the remark of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) with regard to the awarding of mail contracts to school boys. That was wrong, but two wrongs do not make a right.
Yes, but mv hon. friend did not open his mouth when he was sitting on this side of the house.
If it had been mentioned I would have done so.
His name was McConachie.

I am pleased to see that a reduction of $400,000 has been made in connection with air mail service. When reference is made to that service I think, the former Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) should blush. He cannot be made to blush, however.
Not so easily as that.

If I were Postmaster
General to-day I would expend on air mail service not $1,500,000 but less than $100,000. There are only two or three corners in this country where that service is required, one in the far north and another in the far west.
Sir EUGENE F1SET: And the third at Rimouski.

The Post Office Department is supposed to be maintained for service and not for profit. If that be the case the Postmaster General should extend the rural mails throughout this country, though I will confess? to hon. gentlemen opposite that so far I have been unable to secure one route in South Renfrew since this government came into power.

I should like to get some
information with regard to the air mail service. What was the amount expended on air mail service during the year ending March 31, 1931?
The total amount was about $1299,000.

Reference has been made
to the Postmaster General reducing the expenditure on air mail service by some $412,000. Last year the estimate was $1,912,000, of which $1,299,000 was spent; this year the estimate is

Supply-Post Office
81,500,000, so the government has increased by about $200,000 the estimated expenditure for the coming year.
The reason $1,912,000 was estimated as necessary last year was in order to complete the connection of the route from the maritime provinces to Winnipeg via Montreal, either from Montreal to Toronto and from there on to Winnipeg, or from Montreal to the northern part of Ontario and then across to Winnipeg. Tenders were called for to cover that service; tenders were received, and it was estimated that it would require about $478,090 to do the work for the remainder of the year, and that in all the route might cost something like $600,000. That money was not expended by the former government; the contract was not let. The tenders were received and opened three days before the dissolution of parliament, and the awarding of the contract was left in abeyance until after the election. However, the department did spend about $1,299,000 on air service. I know there has 'been some severe criticism of the air mail service, but I believe if hon. gentlemen opposite and perhaps some on this side of the house would go more carefully into the great benefit it has been and will be in future I am sure they will cease their criticisms.
In reply to a question which I asked, the right hon. Prime Minister told the house that the government had the right to cancel existing contracts by giving one month's notice That is quite true, and we were told also that the notice had been given but that it was not the intention to cancel the entire air mail service as established under your humble servant. That month has expired, and I understand that a further notice covering an additional month has been given. I am anxious to know what routes are to be kept up. If this $1,500,000 passes this committee there will be sufficient money to maintain all the routes that were in operation last year.
We desired to link up the east and the west, because until that was done we could not hope to make the air mail service pay. We began in 1928 by establishing an air mail service from Rimouski to Montreal, and by so doing we were able to land transatlantic mail in Montreal more quickly than transatlantic mail could be landed in New York. This placed the business men of the Dominion on an equal footing to the business men of the United States, who formerly received their transatlantic mail from a day and a half to two days sooner than it was received by the north Atlantic route. That meant a great deal to the business people of Canada; it was appreciated by them and they took advantage
of it. Later in the same year we established an air mail service to the northern shores of the gulf of St. Lawrence and carried mail to those people who, in the winter time, formerly had very poor service. We then inaugurated an air mail service to the Magdalen islands, where previously they had not had a service in the winter. That service to the Magdalen islands has paid for itself, and the service on the north shore of the St. Lawrence has paid its way also, if I can judge by the poundage carried. We established air mail service to Prince Edward Island in the winter time when steamship communication was interfered with, and in fact at other times also in order to accommodate the business men of the island. We delivered mail by air from Moncton on a Saturday so that the mail would be distributed to the business houses that afternoon, and on Monday they answered the mail by an outward service. If that had not been done the mail would not have been distributed to them until three o'clock Monday afternoon, so by the air mail we have helped the business men of Prince Edward Island. That service is also paying its way.
We established air mail service to the far-flung sections of the west, up the Mackenzie river into Aklavik, three hundred miles within the Arctic circle, and that service, under a two cent rate, to-day is paying its way and has a surplus. Formerly we delivered mail by dog teams in the winter time and by boat in the summer time, and we paid $41,000 for a service which was of absolutely no use to those people. When we were considering inaugurating air mail service we called for contracts under both systems, the old and the new. There was a difference of only $5,000 or $6,000 between the cost of the air mail service and the cost of the old service, so we adopted the air mail service and instead of giving those people a mail once or twice a year we gave them several deliveries of mail a year. In the Mackenzie district, up to within eight hundred miles of the Arctic, we are giving a service equal to almost any other service in Canada, and to-day that service is more than paying its way. We gave a two cent service in the mining districts of Ontario and Quebec, and every one of them is paying its way to-day. We wished to give a more extended service to the commerce of Canada. We found that American business men, through their air mail service, were getting ahead of our Canadian business men and we therefore established a number of routes such as the route from Halifax to Saint John and then to Montreal, from Moncton to Montreal, from Montreal to Toronto, from
Supply-Post Office

Montreal to Schenectady, from Toronto to Buffalo, and through the prairie provinces. Those routes had a five cent service. They are not paying their way, but the increased volume of business, after the service has been in operation only three years, indicates that within two years it will pay. If it had been possible for me as Postmaster General to link up Montreal direct with Winnipeg, that service would be paying to-day.
Let me appeal to the Postmaster General not to cut out any important branch of the air mail service. I know that the service from St. John and Moncton on to Montreal is not paying, and my hon. friend says it never will pay. Very poor encouragement, coming from a member of the maritime provinces. But that is not so; the service will pay. In the last three months of the last fiscal year the service between St. John and Montreal increased over 30 per cent; and when it is linked up with Halifax, and we have a route from Halifax to Moncton, from Moncton to St. John, and from St. John to Montreal, the service will be used so extensively that it will pay.
Let me now give the figures to show the poundage carried over these routes. On the Amos-Chibougamau route the poundage was 2,224 and the cost $1,200. With that poundage at $1.20 it more than pays the cost. Take the Amos-Simcoe route: the poundage was 3,305 and the cost $1,100. .On the Fort Murray-Aklavik route the poundage was 62,747, to that outlandish and far-flung section of Canada. Over that route we have a postal parcel rate carrying all the furs from that section to civilization. On the Leamington-Pelee island route the poundage is 17,103, and on the Montreal-Alfoany route it is 21,689 pounds of first class matter at $3 per pound. There you have, within $7,000, this important route paying its way. Take the Montreal-Detroit route: the poundage is 39,040. There there was a deficit. The business in increasing, however, and the moment we link up with the network of the American air mail service, getting communication with Mexico, that service will pay its way. Then we have the Montreal-Rimouski route, carrying 53.042 pounds; the Peace River-North Vermilion route, 26,223 pounds, at $120 a pound, the cost being $3,200. Then there is the Quebec-Seven islands, Seven islands-Anticosti-Monc-ton-Magdalen islands route. The cost is $30,000, the poundage being 39,289. This is really two routes in one. Next we have the Narrows-Lake Sioux Lookout, with a poundage of 40,964; the Winnipeg-Calgary-Regina-Edmonton route, newly started, carrying 64,242

pounds. For the Winnipeg-Pembina route I have' not the figures. On the Moncton-Charlottetown route the poundage is 43,846.
What is the cost of the Moncton-Charlottotown route?

That is $15,750. This is only an emergency route used in winter. On the Toronto-Buffalo route there is a poundage of 43,880. With regard to the Montreal-Ottawa route, I may explain that this was only an experiment. I knew at the time that it would not pay and I feel now it will not pay. But it was only once a week and was provided in order to connect with the boat at Rimouski. The Montreal-Quebec route, which is very costly, was also a trial route. When we came to carry out our plans for the Montreal-Queibec route we found we could not call at Quebec and at the same time continue on to St. John and to Moncton, owing to climatic conditions and locations. Quebec was therefore cut out of the general route, but was allowed to remain in for a short time so far as Quebec and Montreal were concerned. We had other routes such as the Lac du Bonnet, with a poundage of 40,715. The air mail service with the two-cent rate has"~more than paid its way.
There is a surplus of between $100,000 and $116,000; and this additional one cent, which I am informed by the Prime Minister will be added to all first class postage, will give another $199,000. The additional one cent added to the five cent rate already established, will give an additional revenue of over $230,-
000.	There you have an additional revenue, by increase in postage over these routes, assuming that the business keeps up. of nearly $400,000. The deficit of the past will amount to about $700,000 in round figures, so that with the extra postage and increased volume of business, this air mail service could be carried on and show a deficit of less than $300,000.
There are gaps in the service between the Atlantic and Pacific coast. One gap is between Sudbuiy and Winnipeg or Toronto and Winnipeg, and the other from Winnipeg to Vancouver. To give a complete service Winnipeg to Vancouver would cost about $370,000 or less per year, and such a service would pay for itself within a very short time. A plane could leave Halifax with 600 pounds of first class matter; it could drop and pick up mail on the way through to the coast, and this complete service could be inaugurated for $3,000,000. I leave it to the officials of the Post Office Department and the Department of National Revenue to verify these figures. This service would pay its way and bring the maritimes 64 hours closer to Vancouver,

Supply-Post, Office
If there is one thing I am desirous of seeing kept up, it is the air mail service. I think I can say without boasting that I had the courage to convince the government of the advisability of putting this service into operation. I saw that our friends to the south were taking advantage of our laxity in extending this service in Canada. I noticed that there was a meeting of financiers in Montreal and Toronto to form companies by which it was hoped to gain control of civil aviation in this country. It was shown that money could be made out of this proposition because these men were interested in air mail and commercial services in the United States, and were hoping to obtain a monopoly of the services in both countries. I knew that the policy of the Department of National Defence was to establish civil aviation in Canada; I felt that an air mail service would be a foundation for commercial and civil aviation, and I recommended that the government put the service into operation. I came before the house in 1928 with this proposal, and it was accepted. I never had anything else but the fullest faith in its success, and I have even greater faith to-day after two or three years of experience.
If Canada takes a retrograde step in the matter of air mail services our friends to the south will try to take advantage of it. At the present time there is an organization in the state of Maine which hopes to inaugurate an air mail service from Boston to Bangor, Bangor to St. Stephen, St. Stephen to Saint John, and Saint John to Moncton and Halifax. They cannot operate an air mail service in Canada without first obtaining the permission of the Post Office Department, and they cannot operate a commercial air service without first obtaining the permission of the Department of National Defence. Has the Post Office Department granted that permission? I am not opposed to its being granted provided it is stipulated that Canada may step in when she is ready to take over the service on the Canadian side. When we are ready we should be able to say: you will stop at the border and we will take the mail through Canada and deliver to you mail from Canada destined for the New England states.
The air mail service offers a means of encouragement to flying. We have to-day in Canada some of the best pilots in the world. Canada is recognized as having the best pilots anywhere. These men made their mark not only during the war but after they returned from the war. American companies are offering higher salaries to our pilots than they receive here, but they showed 22110-265
themselves to be patriots during the war and they are again showing their patriotism by refusing to go to the United States even at a higher salary. If Americans are permitted to establish an air mail service in Canada they will soon attempt to take over the commercial and civil air services and drive our own people out of the business. If this service is permitted to operate between Boston and the maritime provinces I hope the government will take care that it is nothing but an air mail service. These men should not be privileged to do any commercial work; they should be confined to air mail service.
I have made a particular study of this matter. The officials of the department will confirm the fact that I spent many sleepless nights during 1927 and 1928 when we were considering the details of this service. We had the expert advice of the best men in the Department of National Defence and the Post Office Department. When we were not sure of the steps to be taken, our officials went to the United States to investigate conditions there. The American air mail service during its first three years was an utter failure from a financial standpoint. The deficits were enormous because they adopted the wrong system-the poundage system, under which they could not hope to make a financial success. We in Canada, profiting by their mistake, adopted a mileage system. A mileage system prevails in nearly every portion of Canada except in one or two outlying places where hazardous conditions prevail and under our contracts we specify a certain poundage at so much per mile up to that poundage, but above it so much per pound extra. When our United States friends found out that Canada was succeeding so well after its second year in the air mail service, what did they do? We had the pleasure of having our United States friends come to us and consult with officials of the Post Office Department and experts of the Department of National Defence to find out how it was that we were succeeding so well in our air mail service. After they had interviewed the officials I have mentioned, they returned home and changed their whole system. To-day the system adopted, following the Canadian plan, is operating a great deal more to their advantage than the one which they had previously used.
In conclusion let me say I do not mind honest criticism of an enterprise of this kind; I do not mind what criticism may be hurled at me for having inaugurated and undertaken

Supply-Post Office

that system in Canada, but I ask those who feel they should criticize to study first the whole situation as I have laid it before hon. members to-night. It is not very often I am able to say that I agree with the Tory party. I have been a long time in public life; I have been a Liberal by conviction; I have remained so; I see no reason why I should change, and for that reason perhaps my mind may be biased on some of the questions that the party which I am opposing may bring up. But this is one question on which I think we can agree. I urge upon the government that they continue the policy that has already been inaugurated and extend it as necessity requires. If they do so, they will receive my hearty support.
Let me say just one more word in conclusion.
The third conclusion.

If my hon. friend does not like it he can leave. I happen to have the floor, and I do not care whether he likes my way of doing things or not. While I have the floor the hon. gentleman has no right to interrupt me. I think I should say a word on behalf of those who are flying in Canada. Is it known to hon. gentlemen that Canada holds the record to-day for the fastest commercial air service in the world? I am talking now about commercial air service and not of those experts who fly for the purpose of making time. We hold the record of 248 miles an hour in the delivery of air mail, and this was not done for the purpose of making a record. We hold another world record for long distance run of 196 miles an hour. Canada has become famous throughout the world for her splendid pilots, men who were able to attain their present standing by participating in the inauguration of the air mail service of the Dominion.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) on the great task he performed in connection with aerial mail service. He brought out many good points in his speech, however, I must state that if we have found it necessary to modify the policy which he laid down, it is because of economic necessity and also because we have to take into consideration the decrease in revenue of our department due to the crisis which prevails throughout the country. When our finances are in better shape, we shall do our utmost to keep up with the country's progress as regards aerial mail and other matters.
Can the Postmaster General point out what mail routes will be discontinued or will there be any discontinued?

First, there is
the Toronto-BuffaJo route.

There will be
the temporary contracts, such as Montreal-Moncton.

That will be
continued.

Yes. We are
looking into the matter and we have up to August 15, to decide. In the meantime, we shall see what it is possible for us to do.

If you do
not intend to continue, I object to having the appropriations voted.

The previous speaker, the
ex-Postmaster General, made reference in his lengthy remarks on this item to the air mail service between the maritime provinces and Montreal. On that understanding and guarantee the city of Halifax purchased a large strip of land in the western portion of the city and equipped it for the reception of airships, but I regret to say that promise was not carried out.

I cannot let that go by
without correcting the hon. member.

I have listened to the hon.
member for three quarters of an hour.

But the hon. member is
making a statement which is not correct. I have a right to correct it.
I stated that the hon. member promised the people of Halifax he would give them an air mail service if they would provide the proper facilities for an airport.

They had not their port
facilities provided last July.

Supply-Post Office

I did not say anything of
the kind. I said that on the strength of that promise-

How could I keep the
promise if they did not carry out their part?

I will repeat the words of
the right hon. leader of the opposition, Mr Chairman, and ask you to preserve order. I would say to the Postmaster General that the port of Halifax, at great expense to the people of the city, has now provided its part. Representations have been made repeatedly by delegations to the minister and the department from the city of Halifax, the mayor of Halifax, who was here only a few weeks ago, the boards of trade of the city of Halifax and of Dartmouth, Moncton and Saint John with regard to the improvement of the port of Halifax in connection with an air mail service. For these reasons I would ask the minister to take the matter into very serious consideration before making a final decision with regard to the refusal of the department to carry out the promise which was made some time ago to provide an air mail service between Halifax and the cities in the western part of Canada.

I want to ask the Postmaster General a question with regard to a return, No. 253, which was brought down some time ago, and particularly with regard to the mail service on Cape Sable Island. Would the Postmaster General give me the reason why?

I will give my hon. friend
the reasons to-morrow privately, for I have not them here.

Would my hon. friend
also permit me at the same time to ask another question? Perhaps he may get the information with regard to this as well.
